# Solution Messaging Contract

## Purpose
This skill gives revenue agents a vendor-neutral contract for mapping a customer
signal to one credible business motion and one message.
Use it when an agent must decide what to say, which value proposition to lead
with, which proof points are allowed, or how to frame a first step.
The agent applies this contract identically across outreach, account strategy,
and deck work.

## Required inputs
| Input | Required | Accepted source | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Account context | yes | crm, notes | Confirms relationship, segment, active work, and constraints. |
| Trigger signal | yes | crm, workplace, notes, web | Explains why the topic matters now. |
| Audience level | yes | crm, workplace, notes | Sets horizon, proof threshold, and ask size. |
| Runner solution catalog | yes | profile | Limits motions to what the runner can deliver. |
| Sourced proof | conditional | crm, notes, web, decks | Supports claims when proof is available. |
If required input is missing, say what is missing and produce a lower-confidence
recommendation only when fabrication is not required.

## Definitions
A motion is a business change the customer can act on, not a product category.
A trigger signal is observable evidence that a motion may matter now.
A proof point is sourced evidence that the proposed motion has worked, is needed,
or is already relevant to the account.
A first step is the smallest useful action the customer can reasonably accept
without committing to a full initiative.
A disqualifier is evidence that the motion should not be recommended now.

## Catalog check rule
Never recommend a motion the runner's `solution_catalog` cannot deliver.
Never imply a capability unless the runner can name a path to deliver it through
the catalog, a partner, or an approved service route.
If a motion is strategically right but not deliverable, label it as out of
catalog and offer the nearest deliverable alternative.
If no deliverable alternative exists, do not write the message.

## One-idea rule
Every message carries one motion, one business problem, one proof thread, and one
ask.
Multi-motion messages fail because the recipient cannot tell which problem the
sender believes is urgent.
They also force generic proof, make the ask too broad, and sound like a campaign
rather than an informed note.
If more than one motion fits, rank them and write only the highest-confidence
motion.

## Motion family: modernize and migrate
Customer language: aging platforms are slowing delivery, increasing operating
risk, limiting talent flexibility, or making change too expensive.
Typical signals: renewal pressure, data center exit language, end-of-support
risk, merger integration, application backlog, platform reliability issues, or
costly manual operations.
Executive metrics: time to launch, operating run cost, incident rate, technical
debt reduction, resiliency, delivery velocity, and risk exposure.
Proof types that work: sourced before-and-after operating metrics, named
reference patterns from comparable environments, or account evidence showing
current friction.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: identify one workload, dependency, or process where
modernization would remove a measurable blocker.
Traps: leading with infrastructure terms, promising a migration before discovery,
or assuming the customer wants transformation when they need risk removal.
Deleted phrases: "lift and shift everything", "future-proof your business",
"digital transformation journey", and "modern stack" without context.
Disqualifiers: no named platform constraint, no owner for the workload, active
freeze on change, or a better near-term motion around cost, risk, or retention.

## Motion family: unify and govern data
Customer language: teams do not trust the numbers, decisions take too long, data
is duplicated, or compliance and reporting require too much manual work.
Typical signals: inconsistent executive reporting, analytics backlog, fragmented
systems, governance findings, duplicate definitions, slow close processes, or
manual spreadsheet reconciliation.
Executive metrics: decision cycle time, reporting accuracy, audit readiness,
data product adoption, analyst productivity, and time to insight.
Proof types that work: sourced examples of decision latency, documented data
quality issues, or credible benchmark ranges tied to a comparable process.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: choose one decision process and map its source
systems, owners, definitions, and current friction.
Traps: pitching a platform before agreeing on the decision to improve, treating
governance as bureaucracy, or making data purity the business case.
Deleted phrases: "single source of truth" unless defined, "unlock insights",
"data-driven culture", and "democratize data" without a specific decision.
Disqualifiers: no executive decision tied to the data, no accountable data owner,
no appetite to reconcile definitions, or a stronger security or compliance need.

## Motion family: apply AI and automation
Customer language: skilled people are spending time on repetitive work, service
quality is inconsistent, customers wait too long, or teams cannot scale with
current staffing.
Typical signals: service backlog, contact volume growth, manual triage, document
processing burden, high handoff cost, process variance, or public automation
commitments.
Executive metrics: cycle time, cost per interaction, employee capacity, customer
satisfaction, error rate, and throughput.
Proof types that work: sourced workflow baseline, cited automation pattern for a
similar process, or internal account evidence showing a repetitive bottleneck.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: select one high-volume workflow and define the
human review points, data inputs, and success metrics before proposing tools.
Traps: leading with AI novelty, implying headcount reduction, ignoring human
oversight, or making broad productivity claims.
Deleted phrases: "AI strategy", "revolutionize", "autonomous everything",
"replace manual work", and "quick win" when risk is unknown.
Disqualifiers: no process owner, no data access path, unacceptable risk from
automation, unresolved policy constraints, or no measurable baseline.

## Motion family: secure and comply
Customer language: risk is rising, audits are painful, controls are inconsistent,
incidents are expensive, or the business needs to prove trust to customers and
regulators.
Typical signals: incident disclosure, regulatory action, audit findings, control
gaps, cyber insurance pressure, customer security questionnaires, or new data
handling obligations.
Executive metrics: risk reduction, audit findings closed, time to detect, time to
respond, control coverage, and customer trust indicators.
Proof types that work: sourced risk event, documented control gap, or recognized
framework requirement mapped to a customer obligation.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: confirm the highest-risk control gap and identify
the owner, deadline, current evidence, and decision path.
Traps: fear-based selling, overclaiming protection, blaming the customer, or
suggesting urgency without sensitivity.
Deleted phrases: "you are exposed", "breach-proof", "zero risk", "compliance
solved", and "act now before it is too late".
Disqualifiers: no risk owner, privileged details cannot be used, the signal is too
sensitive for outreach, or legal review is required before contact.

## Motion family: optimize cost and efficiency
Customer language: spend is growing faster than value, budgets are tighter,
teams need to fund priorities without adding cost, or leaders need clearer cost
accountability.
Typical signals: expense reduction language, missed efficiency targets, renewal
scrutiny, consolidation work, underused assets, procurement pressure, or budget
holds.
Executive metrics: unit cost, utilization, budget variance, payback period,
forecast accuracy, and productivity per resource.
Proof types that work: sourced utilization evidence, current-state cost leakage
from crm or notes, or public statements about efficiency priorities.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: review one cost pool, usage pattern, or process
owner's spend line and identify avoidable waste.
Traps: sounding like a discount request, implying layoffs, leading with savings
before value, or using generic economic pressure.
Deleted phrases: "do more with less", "slash costs", "right-size everything",
"low-hanging fruit", and "optimization opportunity" without evidence.
Disqualifiers: no visibility into spend or usage, no owner for cost action, the
account is prioritizing growth over efficiency, or savings would damage service
quality.

## Motion family: grow revenue and customer experience
Customer language: growth is harder, customers expect more, conversion is
lagging, retention is at risk, or teams lack a consistent view of the customer.
Typical signals: growth initiative, customer churn concern, product launch,
channel shift, service complaints, sales productivity issue, or loyalty program
change.
Executive metrics: pipeline conversion, retention, wallet share, customer
satisfaction, speed to serve, win rate, and campaign effectiveness.
Proof types that work: sourced customer experience baseline, documented funnel or
service friction, or comparable operating pattern with measurable outcome.
Every proof point must be sourced or omitted.
Smallest credible first step: pick one customer journey moment and define the
current drop-off, delay, or inconsistency.
Traps: promising revenue lift without causality, using vague personalization
claims, or ignoring frontline adoption.
Deleted phrases: "delight customers", "hyper-personalize", "omnichannel
excellence", "growth engine", and "game changer".
Disqualifiers: no customer journey owner, no baseline measure, no route to act on
insight, or a stronger near-term motion around cost or risk.

## Level framing contract
| Audience level | Time horizon | Unit of measure | Proof that counts | Allowed ask |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Individual contributor or manager | Current work cycle | Task, queue, workflow, defect, handoff | Direct account evidence, workflow artifact, or process metric | Validate pain, review one workflow, or identify owner. |
| Director or VP | Current quarter to planning cycle | Team capacity, program outcome, operating metric, risk item | Trend, benchmark, initiative evidence, or cross-team pattern | Align on priority, sponsor discovery, or nominate a workstream. |
| C-level or board | Planning cycle to strategic horizon | Enterprise risk, growth, margin, trust, resilience | Public source, executive commitment, audited metric, or board-level risk | Confirm relevance, agree executive sponsor, or approve a scoped diagnostic. |
For individual contributors and managers, write about friction they can verify
this week.
For directors and VPs, write about operating leverage across a team or program.
For C-level or board audiences, write about strategic exposure or measurable
business outcome, never feature adoption.
The higher the level, the shorter the product language and the stronger the proof
requirement.

## Risk and negative-signal framing
When the trigger is cost pressure, lead with efficiency, not expansion.
When the trigger is a miss, lead with support for a measurable recovery path, not
criticism.
When the trigger is an incident, lead with risk reduction and sensitivity, not
urgency theater.
When the trigger is regulatory action, lead with control evidence and governance,
not a product pitch.
Negative-signal messages must name the customer's problem before naming any
solution category.
If the signal could embarrass the recipient, do not use it directly in outreach.
Use a broader public or operational framing instead.

## Executive credibility rule
An executive message is credible only when it has specificity, a named source, an
ask proportional to the relationship, and no unearned familiarity.
Specificity means the message names the account, signal, business problem, and
motion in plain language.
Named source means every fact points to crm, workplace, notes, web, or decks.
Proportional ask means a cold note asks for confirmation or a short diagnostic,
not executive sponsorship.
No unearned familiarity means no claims about what the recipient feels, wants, or
should care about unless sourced.

## Output contract
Return the selected motion family, confidence, supporting signals, disqualifiers
checked, level framing, proof points used, proof points omitted, first step, and
one message thesis.
If confidence is low, say exactly which input would raise it.
If catalog fit fails, stop and return no motion.
